title: Cap. IX Arg.: Adam's sin remitted to all — God cannot leave anyone in that condemnation by strict right alone
latin: Ab Adae peccato omnibus promiscue remisso sic disputant: Deus non valet stricto jure agere cum ullo homine in communi Adae peccato jacente, ita ut sine ulla spe veniae in ista condemnatione relinquatur: At si reprobaret quospiam tantum ut jacentes in lapsu communi Adae, et non propter actualem eorum et personalem in Deum rebellionem, stricto et summo jure cum illis ageret.
pass_a: From the sin of Adam remitted unto all promiscuously they so dispute: God is not able to deal by strict right with any man lying in the common sin of Adam, so that he be left in that condemnation without any hope of pardon: But if he were to reprobate any only as lying in the common fall of Adam, and not on account of their actual and personal rebellion against God, he would deal with them by strict and highest right.
pass_b: From Adam's sin remitted to all alike they argue thus: God cannot deal by strict right with any man lying in Adam's common sin so as to leave him in that condemnation without any hope of pardon. But if he reprobated any only as lying in Adam's common fall, and not for their actual personal rebellion against God, he would be dealing with them by strict and highest right.

lemmas.gloss: Adam's sin remitted promiscuously to all
cannot leave in condemnation without hope by strict right

title: Cap. IX Arg.: Major confirmed — Adam received; Christ obtained reconciliation for all; therefore reprobation only from final impenitence
latin: Majorem dupliciter confirmare conantur. Primo, exinde quod ipsi Adamo venia data sit: Iniquum enim videatur Deum ob Adami peccatum, quod pura puta illius aestimatione nostrum est, alios quoscunque a vita aeterna excludere, cum ipsum Adamum receperit in gratiam, qui illud peccatum perpetravit. Secundo, idem probare satagunt ex eo quod Christus pro omnibus redemptionem et reconciliationem apud Deum Patrem impetravit; videtur autem parum consentaneum, ut per decretum reprobationis exitio relinquantur, pro quibus Christus ita reconciliationem impetravit, ut nihil impedire possit, praeter impoenitentiam, quo minus ejusdem usu fiant participes. Ergo nemo reprobatur nisi ex consideratione finalis impoenitentiae sive rebellionis tanquam causae motivae: haec autem reprobatio.
pass_a: They try to confirm the Major twofold. First, from this, that pardon was given to Adam himself: For it would seem iniquitous that God on account of the sin of Adam, which by pure mere estimation of his is ours, should exclude any others whatsoever from eternal life, when he received into grace Adam himself, who perpetrated that sin. Secondly, they strive to prove the same from this, that Christ obtained redemption and reconciliation with God the Father for all; but it seems little agreeable that by the decree of reprobation they be left unto destruction, for whom Christ so obtained reconciliation that nothing can impede, besides impenitence, whereby they may become partakers of the use of the same. Therefore no one is reprobated except from consideration of final impenitence or rebellion as moving cause: but this is reprobation.
pass_b: They try to confirm the Major two ways. First: pardon was given to Adam himself — so it would seem unjust that God, for Adam's sin which by mere estimation is called ours, should shut any others from eternal life, when he received into grace Adam who committed that sin. Second: Christ obtained redemption and reconciliation with the Father for all — and it seems little fitting that by a reprobation decree those be left to destruction for whom Christ so obtained reconciliation that nothing but impenitence can bar them from sharing its use. Therefore no one is reprobated except from regard to final impenitence or rebellion as moving cause — and that, they say, is reprobation.

lemmas.gloss: Adam pardoned; others not excluded for his sin alone

title: Cap. IX Resp.: Major false for pagan infants — Augustine Enchiridion 99; Vasquez on infants
latin: Respondeo, Majorem propositi syllogismi quoad infantes Paganorum, qui nec in foedere censentur, nec in Christo regenerantur, aperte falsam esse. Nam si condemnare aliquem ob solum peccatum originale sit stricto jure agere, pertinet est cum talibus agi stricto jure. Atque hinc Augustinus ex catholicae Ecclesiae sententia aperte pronunciat, Universum genus humanum tam justo judicio Divino in apostatica radice esse damnatum, ut etiamsi nullus inde liberaretur, nemo possit recte Dei vituperare justitiam: et qui liberantur sic oportere liberari, ut ex pluribus non liberatis, et in damnatione justissima derelictis, ostenderetur quid meruisset universa consortio: et quo etiam ipsos debitum judicium Dei duceret nisi ejus indebita misericordia subveniret, Enchirid. cap. 99. Quin etiam Vasques Jesuita, qui praedestinationem ex praevisis meritis acriter propugnat, cogitur tamen fateri: Si de reprobatione loquamur qua quis rejicitur a gratia Dei, in parvulis reprobis nullam omnino fuisse suae reprobationis causam; Si de reprobatione, qua quis a beatitudine rejicitur, sermo sit, parvulos eos quibus Divina providentia ita disponit, ut nullum remedium humanae industriae possit adhiberi, fuisse Dei decreto exclusos a regno caelorum, statim post praevisionem originalis peccati ab ipsis contracti, In 1. qu. 23. art. 3. disp. 89. cap. 6. Arminiani igitur longius progrediuntur in defensione erroris sui quam ipsi Jesuitae.
pass_a: I answer that the Major of the proposed syllogism as to the infants of the Pagans, who are neither counted in the covenant, nor regenerated in Christ, is openly false. For if to condemn someone on account of original sin alone is to deal by strict right, it pertains that with such it be dealt by strict right. And hence Augustine from the sentence of the catholic Church openly pronounces that the universal human race by so just a Divine judgment is damned in the apostate root, that even if no one were thence freed, no one could rightly blame the justice of God: and that those who are freed ought so to be freed, that from the many not freed, and left in most just damnation, it would be shown what the universal fellowship had merited: and whither also the due judgment of God would lead even those themselves unless his unowed mercy came to help, Enchiridion chapter 99. Nay even Vasquez the Jesuit, who sharply defends predestination from foresighted merits, is yet compelled to confess: If we speak of reprobation by which someone is rejected from the grace of God, in reprobate little ones there was altogether no cause of their reprobation; If speech be of reprobation by which someone is rejected from beatitude, those little ones for whom Divine providence so disposes that no remedy of human industry can be applied were by the decree of God excluded from the kingdom of heaven, immediately after foresight of original sin contracted by them, On 1, question 23, article 3, disputation 89, chapter 6. The Arminians therefore advance farther in defense of their error than the Jesuits themselves.
pass_b: I answer: as to pagan infants — neither in the covenant nor regenerated in Christ — the Major of their syllogism is openly false. If to condemn for original sin alone is to deal by strict right, then with such God does deal by strict right. So Augustine from the catholic Church's sentence (Enchiridion 99): the whole human race is by so just a divine judgment damned in the apostate root that even if none were freed from it, no one could rightly blame God's justice; and those freed ought so to be freed that from the many not freed, left in most just damnation, it would be shown what the whole fellowship had merited — and whither even they would be led by God's due judgment unless his unowed mercy helped. Even Vasquez the Jesuit, who sharply defends predestination from foresighted merits, must confess: if we mean reprobation as rejection from God's grace, reprobate infants had no cause of their reprobation at all; if rejection from beatitude, those infants for whom providence so disposes that no human remedy can be applied were by God's decree shut from the kingdom of heaven right after foresight of original sin they contracted (on ST I, q. 23 a. 3, disp. 89 c. 6). So Arminians push their error farther than the Jesuits themselves.

lemmas.gloss: whole race damned in apostate root; mercy unowed
even Jesuit: infants reprobated without further cause

title: Cap. IX Resp.: as to adults — God does not damn without foresight of actual sin; reprobation as denying special grace is from liberty
latin: Sed mittamus infantes, et Majorem discutiamus quatenus adultos et rationis ac liberi arbitrii compotes spectat. Quoad tales, si stricto jure agere intelligatur, qui decernit aliquem damnandum et morte aeterna afficiendum sine consideratione peccati actualis, fatemur Deum cum talibus peccatoribus stricto jure haud agere. Hosce enim neque damnavit, neque damnationi destinavit, nisi ob praevisa peccata, et finalem in iisdem impoenitentiam. Verum si per illud, stricto jure agere, Corvinus intelligat, non praeparare gratiam eam specialem, qua adhibita Deus scit atque statuit talem hominem fore liberandum, vel talem hominem praeterire et ad vitam aeternam capessendam decreto specialis providentiae, quam praedestinationem appellamus, haud ordinare, sed suae (ut ita dicam) deficientiae relinquere, tum affirmamus, Deum cum multis sic agere ex sola libertate voluntatis suae: et si hoc sit stricto jure agere (de quo mox videbimus), stricto jure agere cum omnibus reprobis.
pass_a: But let us dismiss infants, and discuss the Major insofar as it regards adults and those having mastery of reason and of free will. As to such, if to deal by strict right be understood as he who decrees someone to be damned and to be affected with eternal death without consideration of actual sin, we confess that God by no means deals by strict right with such sinners. For these he neither damned, nor destined unto damnation, except on account of foresighted sins, and final impenitence in the same. But if by that, to deal by strict right, Corvinus understands not to prepare that special grace, which being applied God knows and establishes that such a man will be freed, or to pass by such a man and not to ordain him unto laying hold of eternal life by the decree of special providence which we call predestination, but to leave him to his (so to speak) deficiency, then we affirm that God so deals with many from the sole liberty of his will: and if this be to deal by strict right (about which we shall soon see), to deal by strict right with all the reprobate.
pass_b: Set infants aside and take the Major as it regards adults with reason and free will. If dealing by strict right means decreeing someone damned and afflicted with eternal death without regard to actual sin, we grant God does not so deal with such sinners. He neither damned them nor destined them to damnation except for foresighted sins and final impenitence in them. But if by dealing by strict right Corvinus means not preparing that special grace which, applied, God knows and decrees will free such a man — or passing him by and not ordaining him to take hold of eternal life by the special-providence decree we call predestination, but leaving him to his deficiency (so to speak) — then we affirm God so deals with many from sole liberty of will. And if that is dealing by strict right (we shall see shortly), then he deals by strict right with all the reprobate.

lemmas.gloss: God does not damn adults without foresight actual sin
Corvinus's strict right = denying special grace

title: Cap. IX Resp.: reprobation decree is secret — reprobates not left without hope of pardon merely by being reprobated
latin: Porro, assumptum illud, quod hisce verbis majori propositioni annectitur, ita ut sine ulla spe veniae in ista condemnatione relinquantur, perperam decreto Dei reprobantis tribuitur. Nam ut praedestinationis, ita et reprobationis decretum arcanum est, nec quantum ad distinctionem singularium ulli mortalium sive quoad seipsum sive quoad alium a priori notum. Sicuti ergo praedestinati, ex eo solum quod praedestinati, spem veniae nondum habent; ita nec reprobati, ex eo solum quod reprobati sunt, sine ulla spe veniae relinquuntur. Nam ut Paulus praedestinatus spem veniae concipere non potuit nisi mediante conversione et fide in Christum; ita nec Judas reprobatus sine spe veniae relinquitur, nisi mediante infidelitate sua et impietate contra Christum. Denique si propter solam eventus infallibilitatem et decreti Divini immutabilitatem Arminiani contendant, quemlibet reprobatum omni spe veniae destitutum, hoc incommodo non minus urgetur ipsorum sententia quam nostra. Nam illi agnoscunt Judam, adeoque singulares omnes homines reprobatos, fuisse ab aeterno fixa et peremptoria Dei sententia reprobatos; ita ut juxta illorum opinionem tam certum, infallibile et definitum fuerit apud Deum, quod Judas veniam et vitam aeternam nunquam consequetur, quam in nostra. Si ergo posita hac reprobatione Arminiana Judas absque omni spe veniae non relinquitur, neque posita illa quam orthodoxi defendunt relinquetur.
pass_a: Further, that assumption which is annexed to the major proposition by these words, so that they be left in that condemnation without any hope of pardon, is wrongly ascribed to the decree of the reprobating God. For as the decree of predestination, so also the decree of reprobation is secret, nor as to the distinction of singulars is it known a priori to any of mortals either as to himself or as to another. As therefore the predestined, from this alone that they are predestined, do not yet have hope of pardon; so neither are the reprobated, from this alone that they are reprobated, left without any hope of pardon. For as Paul the predestined could not conceive hope of pardon except by means of conversion and faith in Christ; so neither is Judas the reprobated left without hope of pardon, except by means of his unbelief and impiety against Christ. Finally if on account of the sole infallibility of the event and the immutability of the Divine decree the Arminians contend that any reprobate is destitute of all hope of pardon, their sentence is urged by this inconvenience no less than ours. For they acknowledge that Judas, and so all singular reprobated men, were from eternity reprobated by a fixed and peremptory sentence of God; so that according to their opinion it was as certain, infallible and defined with God that Judas will never obtain pardon and eternal life, as in ours. If therefore, this Arminian reprobation being posited, Judas is not left without all hope of pardon, neither, that which the orthodox defend being posited, will he be left.
pass_b: Further: the clause annexed to their Major — that such are left in that condemnation without any hope of pardon — is wrongly pinned on the reprobating decree. Like predestination, the reprobation decree is secret; as to which particulars, no mortal knows it a priori of himself or of another. As the predestined do not yet have hope of pardon from being predestined alone, so the reprobate are not left without hope of pardon from being reprobated alone. Paul the predestined could not conceive hope of pardon except through conversion and faith in Christ; Judas the reprobate is not left without hope of pardon except through his unbelief and impiety against Christ. Finally if Arminians argue from mere infallibility of the event and immutability of the decree that any reprobate is stripped of all hope of pardon, that inconvenience presses their view no less than ours. They grant Judas — and so every particular reprobate — was from eternity reprobated by God's fixed peremptory sentence; so that on their view it is as certain, infallible, and defined with God that Judas will never obtain pardon and eternal life as on ours. If, then, on that Arminian reprobation Judas is not left without all hope of pardon, neither will he be on the reprobation the orthodox defend.

lemmas.gloss: reprobation secret; not known a priori of self/other
hope via faith; hopelessness via unbelief — same on both views

title: Cap. IX Resp. to Major's first confirmation: original sin is by contagion, not bare imputation; Adam's penitence was for himself
latin: Jam confirmationem Majoris attendamus. Primo, dicunt repugnare bonitati Divinae, ut immunis sit Adamus qui peccatum ipsum patravit, et alii plectantur, qui mera imputatione rei sunt. Multis vitiis laborat haec confirmatio. Primo, non de plectendis hominibus, sed de reprobandis quaeritur. Aliud enim est reprobatio, aliud damnatio vel punitio, ut saepe inculcavimus. A scopo igitur quaestionis haec verba aberrant. Deinde, nimis extenuant originale peccatum, quando dicunt illud pura puta Dei aestimatione nostrum esse, nosque non aliter quam mera imputatione reos esse. Nam nostrum est, non pura puta imputatione, sed contagiosa propagatione: nec rei tantum sumus mera Dei aestimatione, sed contracta omnium animae facultatum damnabili corruptione. Porro, non repugnat aequitati aut bonitati Divinae, Adamum poenitentem liberare, atque alios in solo originali peccato morientes punire. Nam quae fecit Adamus in statu integro, fecit ut radix generis humani, et tam nobis fecit quam sibi, adeo ut non sibi solum, sed posteris omnibus stetisse et cecidisse dicatur: at quae fecit in statu lapso, sibi fecit, non posteris; nam sibi, non posteris omnibus et singulis, poenitendo gratiam et favorem Divinum dicitur recuperasse. Denique, nec illud iniquum putandum est, quod Deus Adamo uni praeparaverit ac donaverit veram ac seriam poenitentiam ex mera sua misericordia, multis autem ex Adamo prognatis neque praeparaverit neque donaverit eandem poenitentiam salutarem. Nulla enim lege magis tenetur Deus praestare omnibus posteris Adae quod ipsi indulsit, quam exhibere Judae, quicquid Paulo aut Petro ex mera misericordia exhibuit.
pass_a: Now let us attend unto the confirmation of the Major. First, they say that it repugns Divine goodness, that Adam who perpetrated the sin itself be immune, and others be smitten, who are guilty by mere imputation. This confirmation labors with many vices. First, the question is not concerning men to be smitten, but concerning men to be reprobated. For reprobation is one thing, damnation or punishment another, as we have often inculcated. These words therefore wander from the scope of the question. Next, they too much extenuate original sin, when they say that it is ours by pure mere estimation of God, and that we are guilty not otherwise than by mere imputation. For it is ours, not by pure mere imputation, but by contagious propagation: nor are we guilty only by mere estimation of God, but by a damnable corruption contracted of all the faculties of the soul. Further, it does not repugn Divine equity or goodness to free penitent Adam, and to punish others dying in original sin alone. For what Adam did in the intact state, he did as the root of the human race, and he did as much for us as for himself, so that he is said to have stood and fallen not for himself alone, but for all posterity: but what he did in the fallen state, he did for himself, not for posterity; for by repenting he is said to have recovered Divine grace and favor for himself, not for all and singular posterity. Finally, neither is that to be thought iniquitous, that God prepared and gave to Adam alone true and serious penitence from his mere mercy, but to many sprung from Adam neither prepared nor gave the same saving penitence. For by no law is God more bound to furnish to all Adam's posterity what he indulged him, than to exhibit to Judas whatever from mere mercy he exhibited to Paul or Peter.
pass_b: Now their confirmation of the Major. First they say it clashes with divine goodness that Adam who committed the sin be immune while others are smitten who are guilty by mere imputation. That confirmation has many faults. First: the question is not about men to be punished, but about men to be reprobated. Reprobation is one thing; damnation or punishment another — as we have often pressed. So those words wander from the question's scope. Next they too much thin original sin when they say it is ours by mere divine estimation and that we are guilty only by bare imputation. It is ours by contagious propagation, not bare imputation; we are guilty not only by God's mere estimation but by damnable corruption contracted in all the soul's faculties. Further, it does not clash with divine equity or goodness to free penitent Adam and punish others dying in original sin alone. What Adam did in the intact state he did as root of the human race — for us as for himself — so he is said to have stood and fallen not for himself alone but for all posterity. What he did in the fallen state he did for himself, not for posterity; by repenting he is said to have recovered divine grace and favor for himself, not for every posterity. Finally it is not iniquitous that God from mere mercy prepared and gave true serious penitence to Adam alone, and neither prepared nor gave the same saving penitence to many sprung from Adam. No law binds God more to give all Adam's posterity what he indulged Adam than to give Judas whatever from mere mercy he gave Paul or Peter.

lemmas.gloss: original sin by contagion, not bare imputation
saving penitence to Adam alone not owed to all posterity
